title: France closes nearly 400 schools after violent education protests
summary:
About 400 schools in France are expected to stay closed on Friday. Students have been protesting about problems in their schools, and in some places the protests have turned violent.

The protests are about teacher shortages and old, damaged school buildings. They began in the Paris region last month and have spread across the country. Dozens of people have been injured, and police have made hundreds of arrests. The protests and blockades have also become a political flashpoint, which means a point of strong disagreement. The government announced spending cuts in its 2027 budget on Thursday.

Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin told RTL radio, "There is an active and violent minority ... We're not entirely sure that they are even high school students themselves." He said 2,000 people had been arrested since the protests began, with about two-thirds placed in police custody, which means they were held by police.

Education Minister Édouard Geffray said "a little over 400 schools and other educational establishments" would stay closed on Friday. Some of the worst unrest on Thursday was in Marseille, France's second largest city. Public transport there was suspended after staff members were injured. A school was set on fire in the city of Nantes, and another school had fire damage in Le Havre.

In Saint-Denis, near Paris, crowds of young people gathered in front of police. One student held up a sign that read, "Can we explain ourselves without being tear gassed?" Geffray said he would meet representatives of staff unions, parent associations and student associations on Friday.
why_it_matters: Schools are an important part of daily life. This story shows how problems like teacher shortages and damaged buildings can lead to strong protests, and why leaders and students need peaceful ways to talk.
